title: Best Managed OAuth Providers for SaaS Integrations
summary: Managed OAuth for SaaS integrations handles consent and token storage so you don't build it. Compare solutions and pick the one that fits your platform.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces fits in managed OAuth


Think of[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/security) as a workflow platform that manages OAuth connections for its 750 integrations, meaning your existing tools are probably already supported, not a standalone token API.


It fits when the workflow is the product rather than when you only want a vault with a refresh endpoint.


At the architecture level the difference matters, so here's the shape of each side by side.


On the left, a token API sits between your app and the provider. On the right, a workflow platform keeps the connection store inside the engine, embedded in your host app.


Take from it where the refresh logic runs and who your code has to call when a token dies.


*(illustration here)*


### What the docs confirm


When a flow's steps run, Activepieces uses the connections it stores for its integrations (it calls them pieces, and roughly 60% of them are community-contributed). Users create a connection once, and steps reference it by name instead of carrying credentials around.


You can also embed it: the product documents an option to put the builder and connection setup inside your own app and have your customers connect their own accounts.


That's the part that speaks to the "who owns the user experience" question: your app can own the surrounding screens while the platform handles the consent flow and holds the connection.


Where the credentials sit has a second answer. Enterprise plans support secret managers, and credentials are held centrally rather than by each team.


The feature is on the published list, not just in the docs: the Ultimate plan names secret managers alongside SCIM, custom RBAC, audit logs and event streaming, and the enterprise governance feature set lists them next to SSO/SAML.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production. Zapier and Make keep credentials in their own cloud, and neither has a self-hosted edition.


### What it doesn't do


I can't point to docs that describe a standalone endpoint where your backend asks for a fresh access token for an arbitrary provider and gets one back. Treat that as not confirmed, and don't design around it.


If your app code needs to call a provider's API directly, outside a flow, you're working against the grain of the product.


I also can't confirm how it behaves on the boring failures this article cares about.


Check the docs and test, in a staging environment, what happens when a refresh token expires, when a user revokes consent at the provider, and when the provider rate-limits a step.


Look for whether the flow fails loudly, whether the connection is marked broken, and whether anyone is told. Until you've seen that, assume you must build the alerting yourself.


### Who should pick it


Pick it if your integrations already are workflows: a trigger and some steps that use a connection.


It suits teams that want to ship customer-facing automations inside their product without writing each provider's OAuth plumbing, and that are comfortable with tokens living in the platform's store, or in a secret manager they've connected, rather than in their own database.


Skip it if your security team requires tokens in a vault you control and you're not on a tier that supports your own secret manager, or if you need token retrieval as a plain API call.


Those needs point to the standalone token API on the left of the illustration.
